entry.title: A wrong rewrite passed because the global-write log drops word addresses
entry.summary: Verified The checker's comparison of written globals ignores which word inside a declared range each value was written to, so a rewrite that stores the right values at the wrong addresses still passes. A rewrite with one four-word block at the wrong slot offset passed 1188 of 1200 trials.
entry.content:
Verified The checker's comparison of written globals ignores which word inside a declared range each value was written to, so a rewrite that stores the right values at the wrong addresses still passes. A rewrite with one four-word block at the wrong slot offset passed 1188 of 1200 trials.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring functions (a large effect-slot allocator and a small vector routine) and prove each identical to the original with the checker.

What was found

Verified Both functions verified: 1200 trials each, zero failures, non-vacuous, deliberately wrong versions caught for both.

Verified While debugging the large function, its contract declared the whole slot table as one watched range. The worker records every changed word in a range as the range base plus the value, so the verdict compared only the sequence of values, not their addresses. A rewrite that copied one block 96 bytes too low produced the same value sequence on trials where nothing else was written between the two addresses, and passed.

Verified Declaring the table as one single-word range per word restored exact addresses and the same rewrite failed immediately with the true offsets visible. The final contract keeps that shape (679 one-word ranges); no checker code was changed for any verdict.

What was decided or recommended

Record the word address, not the range base, in the globals-write log. Until that lands, contracts covering a table with a single wide range should split it into small ranges so misplaced stores cannot hide. Past verdicts over wide ranges were weaker than they looked wherever a rewrite could shift a block without changing the value order.

How to reproduce it

Declare one multi-word globals range, run a rewrite that writes the range's expected values shifted by one word with nothing interleaved, and observe a pass. Then split the range into one-word ranges and observe the failure with exact addresses.

What was confusing or went wrong

The passing-but-wrong rewrite cost two debug cycles: the value-only log made the misplaced block invisible, and only trials where unrelated writes interleaved between the true and wrong addresses failed, which first looked like a different bug. A second wrong assumption (which helper answer a store used) hid behind the same weak comparison until the ranges were split.

entry.title: Two coverage traps in a 3,394-byte ped-task function
entry.summary: A single-function production lane verified one of the largest functions attempted so far, a ped task refresh routine of about eight hundred instructions and ninety call sites, in twelve hundred trials with zero failures. The rewrite itself was straightforward; nearly all of the debugging time went to two contract traps that other lanes will hit, both found the hard way.
entry.content:
A single-function production lane verified one of the largest functions attempted so far, a ped task refresh routine of about eight hundred instructions and ninety call sites, in twelve hundred trials with zero failures. The rewrite itself was straightforward; nearly all of the debugging time went to two contract traps that other lanes will hit, both found the hard way.

What was asked

Rewrite the function in Rust and prove the rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version five checker, covering every outgoing call and every reachable branch.

What was found

Verified First, the register comparison list is opt-out for method calls, not opt-in. The lane-facing manual describes the list as optional, but the worker compares the object register by default for every method-style callee. Any callee whose register holds a stack address or a leftover value therefore fails until it is explicitly listed with an empty set. Four callees in this function needed that treatment.

Verified Second, fabrication cycles with the same length are phase-locked. Every two-valued null-or-object pin in the first contract was null on exactly the same trials, which made gate-plus-creation combinations structurally impossible and left fifteen callees unfired no matter how many trials ran. The fix was mixed cycle lengths with hand-checked phases so every required combination actually occurs in the trial window.

Verified A supporting check also proved its worth: a stack-depth dataflow over the whole function, using each callee's cleanup behavior from its own epilogue, closed with zero conflicts at every control-flow join, which validated all thirty-five call signatures at once before the first run.

What was decided or recommended

Lanes should explicitly decide the register list for every method-style callee, including an empty list with a reason, rather than leaving it out. Lanes with several nullable inputs should use mixed cycle lengths and verify by hand that each required combination of values occurs at some trial number, instead of assuming more trials will cover it.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contract generator and checker contract for the batch function with twelve hundred trials, then repeat with a second seed; both pass with zero failures and full callee coverage. The deliberately wrong version, which flips one bit of a heap word the original always writes, fails on the heap check as required.

What was confusing or went wrong

The empty-register-list fix was initially misread as the cause of an unrelated failure, because the mismatch display truncates call details to a shared prefix; full per-call logs from a temporary debug print in the lane's own driver copy showed the real divergence. The phase-lock problem survived one full passing run, since the unfired callees only showed up as a vacuous verdict, not a failure.

entry.title: A production batch that caught the manual out
entry.summary: Three task functions were rewritten and verified, and the checker manual turned out to name the wrong key for the return channel.
entry.content:
Three task functions were rewritten and verified, and the checker manual turned out to name the wrong key for the return channel.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighbouring task functions in Rust and prove each one identical to the original through the project's checker, with a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All three rewrites passed one thousand trials each with no failures and no vacuous verdicts, and all three wrong versions were caught.

Verified The manual says the contract's top level return key selects what is compared, but the worker reads the key inside the checks block instead. With only the top level key set, full register contents were compared and dozens of correct trials failed on leftover high bytes. Setting both keys fixed it. The failure mode is fail-closed, but the manual misleads.

Verified The worker's stack comparison does not see scratch writes to the incoming argument slot or below the stack pointer, so functions using those tricks keep the full stack check with no narrowing.

Verified A vehicle data table the code reads is entirely zeros in the untouched executable and is filled in at start-up. Seeding it per trial through the checker's global fills tests the true path; without seeding those trials fault identically on both sides.

What was decided or recommended

  • Set the return channel in both places until the manual is fixed.
  • Seed runtime-filled tables through global fills rather than leaving those branches to fault parity.
  • Show the first diverging call in mismatch reports, not just the first three calls.

How to reproduce it

Run the batch contracts with the stock checker and compare the verdicts with the return key set in one place versus both. Read the named table's entries from the executable image to confirm they are zeros.

What was confusing or went wrong

The checker's verdict detail shows only the first three calls, which looked identical on both sides while the verdict failed; the real divergence was at a later call. A reporting-only addition to a private driver copy exposed it. The driver also overwrote the lane's own results file once; later runs used a separate output folder.

entry.title: An outside review of the pipeline, checked against the machine: five findings, six changes
entry.summary: An outside reader went through the public changelog and argued that the next gains were in the pipeline, not in making lanes write code faster: the memory ceiling, routing work by what the checker can do, the publication scan as a hidden tax, deferrals as queues, and measuring by bytes instead of functions. Each point was checked against the machine before anything was built. Most held, two were larger than the reader could have known, and one led somewhere else.
entry.content:
An outside reader went through the public changelog and argued that the next gains were in the pipeline, not in making lanes write code faster: the memory ceiling, routing work by what the checker can do, the publication scan as a hidden tax, deferrals as queues, and measuring by bytes instead of functions. Each point was checked against the machine before anything was built. Most held, two were larger than the reader could have known, and one led somewhere else.

PointWhat the machine showedStatus
Memory ceilingThe kernel's non-paged pool is at 15.7 GB and still growing; about 20 lanes fit of a target of 52. A census of every open handle found one platform service from the chip vendor holding 81,215 thread handles, 84% of all thread handles on the machine, up from 68,740 eight hours earlier. A thread that has ended stays in kernel memory while a handle to it is open, and so does its process. Over those eight hours the pool grew by about 96 KB per handle that service gained.Handle counts Verified. That the service is the cause is Inferred from the correlation; kernel pool tags cannot be read without administrator rights.
Publication scan as a taxWorse than reported: 737 verified rewrites (131,000 bytes) were sitting in lane folders, out of the repository and out of the verified count. The scan's pattern had no word boundary after a register name, so "test always" and "call chain" read as assembly; and most of the rest were comments noting a calling convention by quoting the return instruction. Only 17 had a match in code.Verified
Route by checker abilityDisassembling all 38,194 game functions takes 14 seconds. 989 functions holding 932,000 bytes very probably pass a double across a call in a vector register, which the installed checker cannot carry: far more than the handful of deferrals had suggested. The scan flags the functions a lane had spent an hour on that morning. Separately, the batch maker's eligibility rule was still the one written for the second version of the checker and was keeping about 1,600 functions out of the queue for abilities added since.Verified (counts); the double label is a heuristic and over-counts somewhat
Deferrals as queues1,046 functions holding 678,000 bytes are deferred and not since verified. Sorted by what would clear them: proven only in stages (64 functions, 181,000 bytes), deferred for lack of lane time (482, 137,000), an indirect call the lane could not route (132, 114,000), doubles in vector registers (95, 108,000), and smaller ones.Verified
Measure by bytesAfter the held rewrites came in: 39% of functions verified but 25.4% of the code by size. Functions of 1,000 bytes and more hold 38% of the game's code and 14.6% of that is verified.Verified
Stalls should raise alarmsTrue, and it had already cost an hour of small-function lanes.Verified

What was changed

  • The scan's pattern now requires a real register or operand, and the importer rewords comments that quote an instruction or bytes of the original. The sanitizer touches comment text only and checks that itself: the text with comments removed must be identical before and after. 715 rewrites entered the repository on the next tick; the verified count rose by that many for this reason and no other.
  • A preflight table records, for every function, what it will ask of the checker. The batch maker holds a function out while it needs an ability the checker lacks, admits the ones the old rule excluded, and writes each function's labels into the batch list so a lane knows at triage.
  • Deferred functions are grouped into queues with the action that clears each, and a new lane kind takes a batch from the largest actionable queue, one lane slot in twelve.
  • Another new lane kind takes only functions of 1,500 bytes and more, two slots in twelve, to find early what the largest functions need.
  • A lane kind that produces no lane while its queue is not empty now raises an alarm that the five-minute status shows.
  • The published progress data carries the share of code verified by size and the share in large functions.

What was not built, and why

  • A scheduler that scores every piece of work by expected bytes, success probability and cost. The measurements it needs now exist (bytes per lane-hour by kind, the queues, the preflight labels); the lane mix is set from them by hand each hour. Automating that choice comes after the labels have a day of data behind them.
  • A shared checker service. Lanes' checker workers are a small part of memory (about 100 MB each, only while a run is in progress); the ceiling is the kernel, not the workers.
  • Leases with checkpoints. A lane's results file and batch list already are its checkpoint; a lane cut off by the service is resumed twice, and whatever an ended lane did not settle goes back to the queue.

What is still the owner's decision

Restarting the vendor's service (or the machine) to release the handles. It is a system service, it needs administrator rights, and the coordinator does not touch it.

To reproduce the handle census: ask the system for every open handle with the object type of each, group by owning process, and look for a process whose thread handles outnumber the machine's live threads many times over.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch through vtable slots and twin diffs
entry.summary: A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions covering rain effects, vehicle audio and vehicle code yielded eighty-four names, with vtable slot joins doing most of the work.
entry.content:
A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions covering rain effects, vehicle audio and vehicle code yielded eighty-four names, with vtable slot joins doing most of the work.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a consecutive run of unnamed functions, with a confidence per name, working from strings, callers, callees and class information rather than reading every function.

What was found

Verified The run splits into rain particle effects code, boat audio code, a materials data loader, train and cable car audio code, radio emitter slots and vehicle class slots, plus thirty-three labels that are not functions.

Verified Dumping the vehicle and audio vtables from the binary and joining slot numbers with already-named sibling overrides named most vehicle slots, including shared base-class implementations used by several classes at once.

Verified Two pairs of near-identical neighbours differ only in where they take an entity from, so one variant serves an external tick and the other an in-update call.

Verified About a fifth of the batch are size-zero inventory labels pointing at mid-function code, jump targets or epilogues; one listed size swallowed four following functions.

What was decided or recommended

Later naming lanes should join vtable slots against prior lane names first, diff near-identical neighbours before reading them, and verify inventory sizes against the first return instruction.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped executable image, build one evidence table of strings, calls and callers for the whole batch, dump the relevant class vtables and match slot numbers to named siblings, then disassemble only the short and unclear functions fully.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three functions funnel into encrypted code so their behaviour stays hidden, and a family of handling float-math helpers was left unnamed because the exact outputs could not be pinned down. Nearest-name caller matches beyond a few dozen bytes proved unreliable and were used only as supporting hints.

entry.title: A dead scan loop and a vector-register gap on the peds-tasks batch
entry.summary: Three of five task-system functions were rewritten in Rust and verified bit-exact over a thousand trials each; the other two were deferred with precise missing checker abilities, and one verified function turned out to contain a scan loop that can never find anything.
entry.content:
Three of five task-system functions were rewritten in Rust and verified bit-exact over a thousand trials each; the other two were deferred with precise missing checker abilities, and one verified function turned out to contain a scan loop that can never find anything.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original through the project's checker, with a deliberately wrong version per function that must fail.

What was found

Verified Three functions passed a thousand trials each with exact float matches and full branch coverage, and every wrong version was caught.

Verified One function's ten-slot result scan is dead code in the original: the slots are zeroed by the function's own stores and no callee receives a pointer to them, so the two inner probe calls can never run. They stay declared and intercepted but exempt from coverage.

Verified One function passes double-precision arguments in vector registers, which the checker cannot transport: the rewrite side moves one word per register while the comparison checks all four. Only all-zero doubles could match, so it was deferred rather than narrowed into a vacuous proof.

Verified One function's main loop is unreachable under call interception: the function zeroes its own loop count and only an intercepted callee could set it back, which stubs cannot do for absolute globals. Only the empty-table path runs, and that alone was not claimed as a proof.

What was decided or recommended

The three passing rewrites were recorded as verified with their narrowings stated. The two deferred functions each got a retry kit naming the exact missing ability: a two-word vector-register transport, and stub writes to absolute globals. A wrong frame-map computation that cost a full attempt is recorded as a caution to re-derive stack layouts from the push and store order.

How to reproduce it

Each verified function ships its contract and verdict files; rerunning the checker driver on any contract reproduces the thousand-trial proof and the wrong-version failure.

What was confusing or went wrong

A single stack-arithmetic slip placed a block of zero stores eighteen hex digits from its true location, which simultaneously misidentified the scan contents, the tail index, and the fill model. The probe failures contradicted the model on all three points at once, and re-deriving the frame map from the instruction order fixed all three together.

entry.title: Naming batch 110: replay cameras, planes, coronas, nav and portals
entry.summary: Verified A batch of 150 consecutive functions split cleanly into eight groups in address order: replay-camera helpers, a shared-memory media channel, particle sample baking, planes and ambient planes, corona light sprites, the nav and path system, camera interpolation, and portal instances. 137 were named, 60 with high confidence.
entry.content:
Verified A batch of 150 consecutive functions split cleanly into eight groups in address order: replay-camera helpers, a shared-memory media channel, particle sample baking, planes and ambient planes, corona light sprites, the nav and path system, camera interpolation, and portal instances. 137 were named, 60 with high confidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 unnamed game functions, with a confidence grade and one sentence of evidence each, working group-first rather than instruction by instruction.

What was found

Verified The batch held complete small subsystems: a plane class with constructor, destructor and damage, control and flight updaters; an ambient-plane manager that streams models and spawns and removes planes; a corona system from texture request through a 768-entry table to render; a nav system with config parsing, cell lookup, work queues and teardown; and portal constructors, destructors and bounds getters.

Verified Four inventory size fields were wrong: two functions listed as hundreds of bytes are tiny jump stubs, one overruns into its neighbour, and one range loop runs past its listed end. Sizes here cannot be trusted past the next function address.

Inferred Several existing symbol names are wrong and were not reused: a supposed script-array function is a plain memory copy by call shape, audio-system names in the nav region sit on code referencing nav data, and a pool constructor carries an animation name while building the portal pool.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the families other lanes already established for camera interpolation, particles and replay code. The next naming lane should diff twin functions against each other instead of reading both, and should treat any callee below the encryption boundary as unverified: several turn out to be allocator and lock stubs identifiable only by call pattern.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch first (calls resolved against merged symbols, imports, string references, mnemonic profiles), then disassemble every short function fully and brief the large ones with entry plus call context. Confirm group membership by disassembling known callers rather than trusting callee names.

What was confusing or went wrong

The encrypted first megabyte makes every low-address callee name suspect, which was only obvious after decoding several and getting garbage. A probe script failed three times on data-section reads that return no bytes; string and constant reads from read-only data worked. Thirteen functions were left unnamed: tiny setters, jump stubs, mode wrappers with unknown modes, and single-field getters whose meaning nothing revealed.

entry.title: Averaging helper reads an uninitialized stack word into its output
entry.summary: Verified One of this batch's task functions writes four output words, and the fourth is whatever happened to be on the stack: the function never stores to that slot. Its in-batch caller never reads the word back, so the garbage goes nowhere there.
entry.content:
Verified One of this batch's task functions writes four output words, and the fourth is whatever happened to be on the stack: the function never stores to that slot. Its in-batch caller never reads the word back, so the garbage goes nowhere there.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the checker, covering the documented edge cases.

What was found

Verified All four rewrites passed twelve hundred trials each with bit-exact float comparison and a caught wrong version per function. While mapping the averaging helper's outputs, its fourth output word traced back to a stack slot the function reserves but never writes: on every call the word leaks one word of whatever the stack held below the call frame.

Verified The proof contract pins uninitialized stack to zero, so both sides read zero there deterministically; the rewrite writes the zero explicitly and the narrowing is recorded. The word is a genuine output of the original, just not a meaningful one.

Inferred The neighbouring selector function calls this helper with scratch memory and checks only the success flag, so the garbage word is harmless on that path. Whether any other caller reads it is unknown.

What was decided or recommended

Record stack-fill narrowing explicitly whenever a rewrite replaces an uninitialized read with the filled value, and check the in-batch callers for whether the word is consumed. Later lanes mapping other outputs of this helper family should assume trailing words may be uninitialized until traced.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the averaging helper and list every store to its frame: three float slots and the count get stored, the slot later copied to the fourth output word does not. Run the checker contract with a defined stack fill and confirm the output word equals the fill on both sides.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two mapping mistakes cost the most time. First, two registers were assumed to hold the same argument where the push count showed they hold different ones; the probe faulted on nearly every trial until the arithmetic was redone. Second, one float store was attributed to the wrong frame slot because a push sits between the address computation and the store; the snapshot comparison caught it on the first probe.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch: zone population, montage music UI, replay records
entry.summary: A batch of 150 consecutive functions split into four clear groups: a zone population density system, the montage video editor music container UI, replay audio event records, and the replay camera. 85 got names and 65 were left unnamed, almost all of them one-instruction shared UI accessors whose field purpose no tracked source defines.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 consecutive functions split into four clear groups: a zone population density system, the montage video editor music container UI, replay audio event records, and the replay camera. 85 got names and 65 were left unnamed, almost all of them one-instruction shared UI accessors whose field purpose no tracked source defines.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name at high, medium, or low confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and leaving the name empty where the purpose cannot be told.

What was found

Verified The population system reads six parallel per-zone density tables through one shared index shape, and the counts it computes feed cop-spawn checks and slot clamps.

Verified The montage clip-tag and music-track lists are stored as obfuscated comma-separated strings that a shared pipeline decodes and tokenizes before use.

Verified Replay audio events come in writer and applier pairs keyed by a one-byte record tag: writers serialize timestamp, entity, and payload from emit handlers, while appliers resolve the handle and replay the event during record processing. Nine tags were mapped.

Verified The frame container classes share one slot-list protocol (array pointer, count, add, remove), and the class-hash virtual slot is used for runtime type checks between frame classes.

Verified Two batch entries are alternate entries or tail continuations of neighbours rather than independent functions: one frontend update reached two bytes into another, and one zone update that jumps into the next function.

What was decided or recommended

One-instruction accessors shared across dozens of UI classes were left unnamed at low confidence, since their mechanical behavior is clear but no source defines what the fields control. The next naming lane covering UI accessors should check whether any caller or override has since given those fields meaning before renaming them. The two entry-sharing pairs should probably be merged in the function queue.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, disassemble each batch entry, and cross-reference string references, import calls, caller names from merged lane symbols, class slot descriptions, and verified rewrite doc comments. A global-reference scan over the whole image finds the consumers of shared state that single-function reads miss.

What was confusing or went wrong

Caller attribution by nearest known name below the call site repeatedly misfired inside long unnamed spans, blaming a UI slot stub or a script native stub for calls made by replay and camera code. Native-mapping names in the merged symbols turned out to be low-confidence lane guesses rather than native-table facts, so they were only trusted where the code shape agreed. The zone data filename could not be recovered because the path buffer lives in a load-state struct shared by many unrelated loaders.

entry.title: Two adjacent task-system functions never return
entry.summary: Verified Two of four neighbouring task-scheduling functions cannot return to their callers: every exit path pops one word fewer than the function pushed, so the return jumps to garbage instead of the caller. The other two functions in the batch rewrote and verified cleanly.
entry.content:
Verified Two of four neighbouring task-scheduling functions cannot return to their callers: every exit path pops one word fewer than the function pushed, so the return jumps to garbage instead of the caller. The other two functions in the batch rewrote and verified cleanly.

What was asked

Rewrite four adjacent task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the checker, at one thousand trials or more per function.

What was found

  • Verified The first and fourth functions verified at 1200 passing trials each, with deliberately wrong versions caught in both cases.
  • Verified The second and third functions each push one stack word more than any of their exits pop. Counting pushes against pops on every path to a return shows all exits are short by exactly one word.
  • Verified The third function therefore resumes at whatever its caller's saved register held. Setting that register to two distinctive values in two probes produced faults at exactly those two addresses.
  • Verified The second function resumes at a frame-local value instead; a probe faulted at an unmapped garbage address that matches neither the return address nor the checker's blank-stack pattern.
  • Inferred Each broken function has a single caller that expects a normal return, so any in-game call reaching an exit either crashes or runs wild. Whether those call paths are live or dead is unknown.
  • Inferred A leftover register save plus a dead constant store just above it suggest a bad hand edit added the extra push without fixing the exits.

What was decided or recommended

  • Both functions were deferred as unverifiable: a rewrite can only match them by jumping to the same garbage, and the checker has no notion of a wild jump as correct behaviour. The jump target of the third function (an incoming register) is additionally unobservable to a rewrite.
  • Full retry kits were kept: analysis, contracts, rewrites and the fault verdicts, so a future lane can resume if wild-jump verification is ever defined.
  • Recommended for other lanes: balance-check every exit (pushes versus pops on each path to a return) before writing a contract. A push with no matching pop means the function never returns. A two-trial probe with a pinned register value confirms it in under a minute.

How to reproduce it

  1. Disassemble each function and count frame pushes against pops plus cleanup on every path that reaches a return.
  2. Run the original under the checker with the incoming register pinned to a distinctive value and a stubbed gate callee; read the fault address from the verdict.
  3. Repeat with a second distinctive value and confirm the fault address follows it.

What was confusing or went wrong

The stack pointer value after the return looked almost right (one word low), which first suggested a mere cleanup mismatch that the usual check switches could cover. It took a second look to see the popped return address itself was garbage, which is a different and fatal defect. One build also failed briefly because the previous probe's worker process still held the rewrite library; a retry seconds later worked, and no stray processes were left running.

entry.title: A whole family whose listed starts land inside the true functions
entry.summary: Five functions handed to one production lane turned out not to be functions at all: every listed start lands in the middle of a real function, and four of them land in the middle of an instruction. Underneath sits a family of seventeen identical dispatch thunks, sixteen of which were rewritten and verified.
entry.content:
Five functions handed to one production lane turned out not to be functions at all: every listed start lands in the middle of a real function, and four of them land in the middle of an instruction. Underneath sits a family of seventeen identical dispatch thunks, sixteen of which were rewritten and verified.

What was asked

Rewrite and verify five neighbouring functions in the pedestrian task subsystem, each a few hundred bytes, on the stock checker.

What was found

Verified None of the five listed addresses is a function entry. One points at an instruction boundary partway through a function, just after its setup call; the other four point into the middle of instructions. A scan of the program found no caller targeting any of the five, contradicting the inventory evidence attached to them.

Verified The true functions are seventeen consecutive instances of one template: a small setup call, a handler looked up once by a numeric id and then cached, optional pre and post observation hooks, the handler call with the arguments forwarded unchanged, and a use-count decrement. Members differ only in the id, the cache slot and the argument count (two to five).

Verified The function inventory has no entries at any of the seventeen true starts; instead it tiles the region with chunks beginning mid-function, absorbing each true prologue into the previous chunk. The same wrong starts appear in the automated analysis output.

Inferred Each thunk wraps one handler id in what looks like a task-dispatch table, but the slots it reads have no known names, so the names remain proposed.

Unknown One virtual-table slot in read-only data points into the middle of one thunk. Either the game really vectors a call there or the table attribution is off; telling which needs a running game.

What was decided or recommended

  • The five listed starts were recorded as not-a-function with the exact true entry for each, and the sixteen true functions spanned by the batch were verified instead (twelve hundred trials each, every one with a wrong version the contract catches).
  • Recommended: the inventory should gain the seventeen true entries and drop the mid-function fragments, or every lane handed one of these starts will hit the same wall.
  • Recommended: a second look at the virtual-table slot that points mid-thunk before its name is trusted.

How to reproduce it

Decode any listed start through the executable's mapped image: there is no prologue, and the bytes just before it complete the previous thunk's shape. A generator that asserts each member's shape (one direct call, three shared-slot calls, one cached-handler call, the id pushed three times) and emits the rewrites and contracts reproduces the sixteen verifications.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first probe failed on a call-time snapshot: the original showed two zeroed words where the rewrite showed a zero and garbage. The snapshot is taken before the scripted callee writes land, and two separate locals in the rewrite are not guaranteed adjacent, so the second word was uninitialised stack. Passing one explicit two-word array fixed it. Any out-parameter wider than one word needs an explicit array or struct in the rewrite.

entry.title: Eight ped-task builders verified, and one stores uninitialised stack
entry.summary: A production batch of eight pedestrian-task builder functions was rewritten in Rust and all eight were verified against the original, with one genuine quirk found: a slot-registration function writes an unstaged frame word into its global table.
entry.content:
A production batch of eight pedestrian-task builder functions was rewritten in Rust and all eight were verified against the original, with one genuine quirk found: a slot-registration function writes an unstaged frame word into its global table.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of eight medium-sized functions from the pedestrian-tasks subsystem and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, including a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All eight rewrites passed twelve hundred trials each with zero failures, bit-exact floats throughout, and every wrong version was caught.

BehaviourCount
Task builders sharing one validate-allocate-construct-assign shape7
Slot-registration function with trigonometry helpers1
Distinct call-sequence shapes observed passing58
Trials ending in matching faults on both sides750

Verified The slot-registration function stores one word into its global table from a frame slot that nothing ever writes. Under a zero stack fill the original writes zero there, and the comparison confirms it. This looks like an uninitialised read in the original rather than a deliberate zero.

Verified A drive-task builder keeps its height argument when it is above minus one hundred or when it is not-a-number, because the below-jump is taken on unordered comparisons. An early rewrite that treated not-a-number as below failed exactly those trials.

Verified The task-assign helper takes its arguments in the order handle, task, slot. The push order reads slot first, which misled the first rewrite until the call comparison failed.

Inferred Three builders normalise angles by looping add or subtract three-sixty; infinite inputs would loop forever in the original, so they were excluded from the inputs and the exclusion is recorded per function.

What was decided or recommended

  • The uninitialised store is reproduced as a literal zero with the reasoning recorded in the rewrite, since the original provably writes zero under a defined fill.
  • Pool-lookup answers were kept always live, so the fault path for a null lookup answer stays unexercised; a later fault-parity probe could close that gap for the whole family.
  • Neighbouring task builders can clone these contracts: the validate-allocate-construct-assign shape, the frame-pointer snapshot pattern, and the exact float-truncation emulation repeat across the subsystem.

How to reproduce it

Each function has a contract generator that asserts every call-site address and per-callee site count, a contract, a rewrite, and a verdict file in the lane scratch folder. Rebuilding the rewrite crate and running the stock checker driver over the eight contracts replays all ninety-six hundred trials plus the eight wrong versions.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two hand-computed frame offsets were wrong by a few bytes each (hexadecimal addition done from memory), and both were caught by failing probes before anything shipped. Frame arithmetic for these contracts is now done with a script, and the generators assert the resulting site map. The first rewrite of the drive-task builder also missed the unordered-comparison behaviour above, which the not-a-number trials caught immediately.

entry.title: production batch: three task functions verified, one deferred on an unservable read
entry.summary: A production batch of four neighbouring task-system functions yielded three verifications and one deferral, plus a checker robustness finding: the guard that should make unrelocated reads fault loudly is silently absent on this machine, so one function reads ambient memory instead.
entry.content:
A production batch of four neighbouring task-system functions yielded three verifications and one deferral, plus a checker robustness finding: the guard that should make unrelocated reads fault loudly is silently absent on this machine, so one function reads ambient memory instead.

What was asked

Rewrite four medium and large task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version 5 checker, at least one thousand trials per function, with a deliberately wrong version per function and an honest account of what each proof does not cover.

What was found

Verified Three functions passed twelve hundred trials each with zero failures, every declared callee firing and every wrong version caught: a task-set refresh with four member loops, a task dispatcher with an indirect handler predicate and a table-walking loop, and an aim update with two scripted phases, two arctangent calls and a flag forest folded into a bitfield.

Verified The fourth function reads one byte of writable game data through an address with no relocation entry, on two major paths. A minimal probe reaching the first read showed the original does not fault: the memory guard that should catch such reads cannot be established on this machine, so the original silently reads whatever the operating system mapped there. The value is unservable (writable data the shadow mechanism could not provide anyway) and meaningless to reproduce, so the function was deferred with the read documented.

Verified Two smaller checker behaviours cost attempts and are worth one line each in the manual: callees using the register convention compare that register by default unless explicitly skipped, and constants baked into instructions may be relocated by the test harness, in which case the rewrite must relocate them too.

What was decided or recommended

  • Three functions ship as verified with their narrowings disclosed (uncompared vector-register inputs to the arctangent calls, one unmodelled stride word at the out-word cap, a stack check off where the original rewrites its own argument slot, allocator callees modelled as no-ops, cookie checks left native).
  • The fourth is deferred as needing an unavailable checker ability, with the probe kept so the next lane continues instead of starting again.
  • Recommended: the worker should record whether its memory guard is actually up, or refuse to run functions with unrelocated accesses when it is down. A rewrite that copies the raw read would currently match byte for byte against ambient garbage and look verified.

How to reproduce it

Run the stock version 5 worker against the three shipped contracts for twelve hundred trials each; all pass with every callee firing. Run the ten-trial probe contract for the fourth function: the original completes without faulting and takes the branch for a nonzero byte, while a rewrite that refuses to mirror the raw read diverges exactly there. Inspecting the worker source shows the guard reservation ignores failure, which is the mechanism.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two rewrite bugs came from resolving stack-relative operands at the wrong stack-pointer value (before versus after call cleanup); both were caught by failing trials within minutes. A misread instruction address on the fourth function sent the first probe at the wrong patch site; the generator now asserts every site holds a call opcode before writing the contract. Build locks from lingering short-lived processes cleared on their own; no lane processes were left running.

entry.title: Two latent bugs in one batch of task functions
entry.summary: Rewriting six neighbouring task-system functions turned up two genuine defects in the original program: a list-removal routine that deletes about half the remaining entries instead of one, and a state-dispatch branch that cleans four bytes too many off the stack and then returns into garbage. Both were proven with the checker, not guessed.
entry.content:
Rewriting six neighbouring task-system functions turned up two genuine defects in the original program: a list-removal routine that deletes about half the remaining entries instead of one, and a state-dispatch branch that cleans four bytes too many off the stack and then returns into garbage. Both were proven with the checker, not guessed.

What was asked

Rewrite six medium-sized task functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original, with at least a thousand trials per function and a deliberately wrong version per function to show the proof can tell right from wrong.

What was found

Verified All six rewrites passed a thousand trials each with no failures, and all six wrong versions were caught.

Verified The list-removal routine converges both ends of its shift loop, so removing an entry shortens the list by roughly half the tail rather than by one, and a match in the last slot removes nothing at all. The rewrite copies the behaviour exactly and the checker confirms it.

Verified One dispatch branch pushes four words for a call and then discards five, leaving the stack one word high so the function returns into its own argument. Every trial that took the branch faulted at exactly that address. That branch has no defined behaviour, so the proof covers everything except it and says so.

Inferred The six functions share one per-task block of offsets and call into each other, which supports the inventory's guess that they form one task subsystem.

What was decided or recommended

Replicate observable quirks verbatim rather than fixing them, and exclude crashing paths from proofs loudly instead of weakening the comparison. Future lanes should generate addresses by script, re-derive stack frames after every push in each branch, and intersect rotating test phases on paper before running.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's six checker contracts from its scratch folder; the verdict files record the thousand-trial passes. The removal quirk shows as a count dropping by more than one after a single match, and the stack defect shows as a fault at the address held in the first argument on every trial that takes the gated branch.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three self-inflicted delays: a script bug that misread the relocation table, a hand-written address missing a digit that patched into encrypted code and hung trials for minutes, and a tail disassembly started at the wrong byte that invented an instruction. Each was caught by re-reading bytes rather than trusting listings.

entry.title: A float compare idiom tests equality, not unorderedness
entry.summary: Three box-test functions in one production batch share a machine-code pattern that looks like an unordered-operand check but is really an equality test: the branch is taken unless the value compares equal to zero, so the correct rewrite is a not-equal comparison, not an is-not-a-number test.
entry.content:
Three box-test functions in one production batch share a machine-code pattern that looks like an unordered-operand check but is really an equality test: the branch is taken unless the value compares equal to zero, so the correct rewrite is a not-equal comparison, not an is-not-a-number test.

What was asked

Rewrite eight neighbouring ped task functions and prove each rewrite identical to the original over at least one thousand trials with the version 5 checker, with one deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All eight rewrites passed twelve hundred trials with zero failures and non-vacuous verdicts, and all eight wrong versions were caught.

Verified The pattern compares a float against positive zero, loads the flags into a byte register, masks the zero and parity bits, and branches on the processor parity flag. Parity of that masked byte is even exactly when the two flag bits agree, which happens for unequal-ordered and unordered results alike, and fails only for ordered-equal. The branch therefore skips unless the value is ordered-equal to zero: either signed zero passes, while any nonzero or not-a-number value fails.

Compared valueBranch outcome
Positive or negative zeroFalls through (counts as match)
Any nonzero numberSkips to next candidate
Not a numberSkips to next candidate

Verified A rewrite using an is-not-a-number test failed six of sixty probe trials; replacing it with a not-equal-to-zero test passed the full twelve hundred. A signed-zero trial confirmed negative zero still matches, and a not-a-number trial confirmed it still skips.

Verified Same-period contract cycles can phase-lock so that a conjunction of conditions never holds on any trial: one function's fallback-store mutant passed one hundred of one hundred runs until the cycle lengths were decoupled, after which it failed as required.

What was decided or recommended

Transcribe the compare, load-flags, mask and parity-branch sequence as a not-equal-to-zero test. When a contract cycles several independent conditions, give them different periods and check by hand that every path's conjunction has a solution.

How to reproduce it

Build any contract exercising the pattern with a nonzero ordered miss marker and a point outside every box: the original rejects the node. A rewrite testing only for not-a-number accepts it. The lane's contracts pin box coordinates, marker values and list shapes so that match, miss, empty-list and signed-zero paths all run.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first reading of the idiom as an unordered check survived three reviews of the logic because the parity flag reuse is genuinely subtle; only the failing trials forced a re-derivation from the flag definitions. A hand-computed constant in the same contract turned out to be negative infinity rather than the intended quiet not-a-number, which briefly muddied the diagnosis; both values are now in the cycle under correct labels.

entry.summary: A batch of 150 consecutive functions turned out to be mostly the ped task system: virtual methods of task classes, their constructors and destructors, and small helpers around sitting, swimming, doors and movement. 145 of the 150 got names, most at high confidence.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 consecutive functions turned out to be mostly the ped task system: virtual methods of task classes, their constructors and destructors, and small helpers around sitting, swimming, doors and movement. 145 of the 150 got names, most at high confidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name and no guessing.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into five groups: wrappers that build a task and hand it to a ped, script-native registration tables, a refcounted table of loaded script programs, one constructor and destructor per task class, and the task virtual methods (clone, sub-task creation and control) with their helpers.

Verified The meanings of the task virtual-table slots were confirmed by cross-referencing prior lanes: dozens of earlier names agree that the first slots are clone, task id and abort handling, and that the complex-task tail is create-next, create-first and control. That one table named most of the batch.

Verified Seven already-verified constructor rewrites carry audio-subsystem names but are really task constructors: each is called only from one task clone routine and installs that task class table. The rewrites match the bytes, so only the names are wrong. Left untouched for the coordinator to decide.

Verified Six registration routines install 182 script natives in themed groups such as weapons, fire, zones, rendering and time. A full scan found just over three thousand registrations; some point at a shared stub, presumably removed natives.

Inferred Three small list helpers look like methods of the 16-slot task list (append, destroy all, clone from), based on exact layout match and callers, but the list table holds only a destructor, so they would be non-virtual. Kept at medium confidence.

Unknown Five functions were left unnamed: two registered script natives whose implementations lead into encrypted code or an unidentified routine, and three tiny virtual-call chains with no discernible purpose.

What was decided or recommended

Named 145 functions: 105 high confidence, 40 medium, 5 empty. Recommended follow-ups: build a native-id to native-name table (a web search failed and the id is not a plain name hash), extend the task-id table (several ids seen here are missing), settle the task-id versus task-type wording, and review the seven mislabelled constructor names.

How to reproduce it

Decode each function through the mapped executable image and compare instruction counts with the inventory as a mapping check. Collect, per function, its direct calls resolved against merged lane names and verified rewrites, any strings and tables it references, and which routines call it. Cross-reference virtual-table targets against earlier naming results to fix slot meanings before naming any virtual method. For registration routines, pair each implementation address with its hash and resolve the implementations through known native names.

What was confusing or went wrong

Several inventory sizes overrun into neighbouring functions, including two entries that overlap each other, so entry sizes had to be re-derived from the code. The release paths of the script table fall through to a null access on empty slots, which reads as a deliberate trap rather than a bug. One append helper appears to delete its argument on the full path in two layers, which would be a double free, but pool behaviour is unknown so it is recorded as an oddity only.

Propose descriptive names for 150 unnamed game functions in address order, with a confidence per name and evidence for each.

entry.title: A player-ped routine reads an uninitialized stack slot
entry.summary: One verified routine in the peds-tasks batch passes four numbers to its motion sink, but only computes three of them: the fourth word is loaded from a stack scratch slot the routine never wrote, so whatever the caller left there becomes part of the output.
entry.content:
One verified routine in the peds-tasks batch passes four numbers to its motion sink, but only computes three of them: the fourth word is loaded from a stack scratch slot the routine never wrote, so whatever the caller left there becomes part of the output.

What was asked

Rewrite six neighbouring peds-tasks routines in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the project checker, which runs both sides from identical starting state and compares calls, memory and results.

What was found

Verified All six routines verified at 1200 trials each with distinct wrong versions caught. While contracting the player-ped motion-blend routine, its fourth output word traced back to a stack slot below the incoming stack pointer that nothing in the routine writes. A control run with a zero stack fill passes; the same contract with a 1.0 fill fails exactly the trials that take the computing path, which confirms the word is whatever the stack held.

Verified Two smaller quirks in sibling routines: a chain scan recomputes the same priority value twice and compares it against itself, so two of its branches are dead; and a probe float is compared against a live copy that no scripted callee can change, so the unequal path is reachable in the harness only through NaN inputs.

What was decided or recommended

The rewrite stores zero for the uninitialized word with a comment, and the proof is recorded as covering the zero-fill behavior only. Any future caller of this routine should treat that fourth word as meaningless rather than as a computed value. The dead branches and the NaN-only path are implemented faithfully and noted in the results.

How to reproduce it

Run the routine's proof contract with the stack fill set to zero and confirm it passes, then set the fill to the bit pattern for 1.0 and confirm that exactly the computing-path trials fail in the sink-call snapshot. Both runs use the stock checker worker and the committed contract for the lane's fifth routine.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early relocation script double-added the page base and reported every absolute operand in the batch as unrelocated, which briefly made the whole batch look unverifiable; the corrected check shows all of them have relocation entries. Separately, a pushed constant that carries a relocation entry must be relocated in the rewrite too, or the call log differs; that cost one failed probe before the pattern was clear.

Propose a descriptive name at high, medium or low confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and naming each function from strings, imports, known callers and callees, and class context.

Propose a descriptive name with confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first.
